chief_complaint: recurrent gross hematuria following upper respiratory infection
hpi_details: A 29-year-old male presents with a third episode of gross, cola-colored hematuria in the past year, this time appearing within a day of developing a sore throat and nasal congestion. The hematuria resolves on its own after a few days between episodes, and he otherwise feels well, denying joint pain, rash, or abdominal pain.
ideas: He thinks the severe cold spread into his urinary tract or that coughing hard broke a blood vessel down there.
concerns: He is worried he might have bladder cancer like his uncle did, especially with the dark blood returning multiple times.
expectations: He hopes to get a urine test and some strong antibiotics today so this infection finally stops flaring up.

investigation_events.title: Urinalysis with microscopy
investigation_events.availability_message: The urinalysis and microscopy results are now available. Additional protein quantification and specialist testing remain follow-up investigations.

results.value: 2+ blood, trace protein, and a few red blood cell casts

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of IgA Nephropathy is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management centers on confirming the diagnosis and optimizing supportive care with blood pressure and proteinuria control (ACEi/ARB); routine corticosteroids are reserved for selected high-risk patients after optimized supportive therapy, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: recurrent gross hematuria following upper respiratory infection

Key HPI features: A 29-year-old male presents with a third episode of gross, cola-colored hematuria in the past year, this time appearing within a day of developing a sore throat and nasal congestion. The hematuria resolves on its own after a few days between episodes, and he otherwise feels well, denying joint pain, rash, or abdominal pain.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: BP 128/82, HR 74, afebrile. Mild pharyngeal erythema consistent with recent URI. No rash, no joint swelling, no peripheral edema. Urinalysis: 2+ blood, few RBC casts, trace protein. Serum creatinine and complement levels normal.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out IgA Nephropathy.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Rising creatinine or heavy proteinuria.
management_principles: Optimize supportive care with an ACE inhibitor or ARB for blood pressure and proteinuria control, and monitor protein excretion
Consult nephrology; consider corticosteroids only in selected high-risk patients after optimized supportive therapy, not routinely
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

source_refs.title: KDIGO 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline for Kidney Disease

reference_soap.subjective: 29M presents with a third episode of gross, cola-colored hematuria in the past year, this time appearing within a day of developing a sore throat and nasal congestion. The hematuria resolves on its own after a few days between episodes. Denies joint pain, rash, or abdominal pain.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: BP 128/82, HR 74, afebrile. Mild pharyngeal erythema consistent with recent URI. No rash, no joint swelling, no peripheral edema. Urinalysis: 2+ blood, few RBC casts, trace protein. Serum creatinine and complement levels normal.
reference_soap.assessment: Recurrent synpharyngitic gross hematuria with RBC casts and normal complement levels, classic for IgA nephropathy.
reference_soap.plan: Confirm diagnosis and risk-stratify with urinalysis, kidney function, quantified proteinuria, and nephrology assessment; biopsy is often needed when the diagnosis or prognosis is uncertain. Optimize supportive therapy with blood-pressure/proteinuria control. Do not use systemic corticosteroids routinely; consider them only in selected high-risk patients after optimized supportive care and specialist review.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of IgA Nephropathy
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for IgA Nephropathy
Implement evidence-based management plan: ACEi/ARB, monitor protein excretion, steroid trial if severe

teaching.one_liner: IgA immune complex deposition in the glomerular mesangium causes recurrent visible blood in the urine, classically within a day or two of an upper respiratory infection.

must_ask.say: Does the blood appear within a day or two of a cold?
How many times has this happened?
Do you feel normal between episodes?
Does kidney disease run in your family?
Do you have high blood pressure?

history.answer: I caught a cold yesterday, and starting this morning my urine turned dark red like cola.
This started earlier today. It's actually the third time this has happened over the past year, and the previous episodes went away on their own after three or four days.
It looks dark brown and cola-colored, not bright red, and I haven't seen any blood clots.
The dark color is present throughout the entire time I pee, from start to finish.
No, I haven't felt any pain when the blood appears or while urinating.
No, I don't have any pain in my flank, back, or groin area.
No burning sensation when I urinate, and I am not going to the bathroom more frequently or urgently than usual.
No, I haven't had any fever, chills, or night sweats.
No, my stream is strong and normal, with no trouble starting or feeling like urine is left behind.
No swelling in my eyelids or legs, no frothy bubbles in the toilet, and the total amount of urine seems normal.
My sore throat and runny nose started yesterday, and the cola-colored urine appeared within twenty-four hours. I haven't had any skin infections or sores.
No rashes, no joint pain or swelling, and no cough or coughing up blood.
No, my weight has been completely steady and I have not felt unusually fatigued.
No nosebleeds, no bleeding gums, and I don't bruise easily.
No, I do not take aspirin, blood thinners, or any medications that affect clotting.
No intense workouts lately, no trauma or blows to my back, and I haven't eaten beets or taken rifampin.
I work in an office, so I haven't had any exposure to industrial dyes, rubber, or toxic chemicals.
Between these episodes I feel completely healthy and normal, and my urine clears up completely.
My blood pressure has always been normal whenever I've had checkups.
I thought maybe this awful cold spread down to my bladder, or I strained so hard coughing that I burst a blood vessel.
I'm terrified this might actually be bladder cancer like my uncle had, since seeing that dark blood keep coming back really scares me.
I'm hoping you can check my urine and give me a course of strong antibiotics so this stops happening every time I catch a bug.
I have no history of chronic medical conditions, kidney disease, or kidney stones.
I have never had any surgeries and have never been hospitalized.
I am not taking any prescription drugs, over-the-counter pain relievers, or herbal supplements.
I don't have any known drug allergies.
I have never smoked cigarettes.
I only drink socially, about one or two beers on occasion.
I work an office job in IT and live in an apartment with a roommate.
Nobody in my family has kidney disease, kidney failure, dialysis, or early hearing problems.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 128/82 mmHg, heart rate 74 beats per minute, afebrile at 36.8°C.
Mild pharyngeal erythema without tonsillar exudate; nasal mucosa is mildly congested.
Abdomen is soft, non-tender throughout, with no palpable mass or suprapubic fullness.
No pretibial edema or periorbital puffiness noted.
No purpura, petechiae, ecchymoses, or active rashes on the skin.
No swelling, warmth, tenderness, or limitation of motion in peripheral joints.
Prostate is normal in size, smooth, and non-tender without palpable nodules.
